summary: This work demonstrates optical-assisted transmission of microwave control signals for superconducting qubits, modulating XY and Z control signals on a 1490 nm directly modulated laser at room temperature and regenerating them with InGaAs photodiodes at the 4 K stage of a dilution refrigerator. Single-qubit and two-qubit CZ gates achieve fidelities of 99.915% ± 0.005% and 99.676% ± 0.041%, respectively, meeting surface-code error-correction thresholds while reducing heat load and enabling thousand-channel scalability.
motivation: Scaling superconducting quantum processors to thousands of qubits faces a critical bottleneck: the growing number of microwave control cables creates excessive heat load and spatial constraints in dilution refrigerators. Optical transmission offers dramatically reduced passive heat load compared to coaxial cables (5.6 μW versus ~1 mW at 4 K per line), enabling orders-of-magnitude improvement in channel density.
method: A directly modulated distributed feedback laser at 1490 nm carries IQ-mixed XY signals and Z square-wave pulses from room temperature through optical fiber to InGaAs PIN photodiodes (reverse-biased at 1 V) mounted at the 4 K stage, which regenerate microwave control signals. Gate optimization uses standard Ramsey and cross-entropy benchmarking techniques; noise is characterized via RTO and CPMG sequences on the qubit and room-temperature instrumentation spanning 10$^{-3}$ to 10$^7$ Hz.
result: Measured $T_1 = 58.58 ± 3.39$ μs and $T_2^* = 2.40 ± 0.23$ μs; single-qubit 50 ns X/2 gates with control error 0.004%–0.023%; two-qubit 38 ns CZ gate with control error 0.053%; Z-line noise floor ~0.04% idle-gate error at 10$^{-3}$ Hz; thermal analysis shows 4 K stage can support ~2000 channels for XY+Z control, matching the $P_C/P_L$ ratio of 1996 for the Bluefors XLD400 refrigerator.
